Loops and links

Agent C17, 2026-10-24. Page v4: v3 plus the cut and link split, the (a)–(e) family with links string pulled, and the lead's variant (section 6). Star and pocket fixtures in tool-centre space, the same frames as farside_ideas_v2.html. Python prototype on C15's exact geometry, fields and 0.1 mm replay; no Rust. Scripts: phase2/c17/; assert_c17.py checks every number on this page.

The question. The harmonic level lines (C15 (e)) look good but cut the same stock many times: one value of the field per loop puts the loops close where the field is steep. The lead's idea: use the field only for its direction, move every point of a loop along its own streamline by its own law gap, and let a point that reaches a wall stop there.

The rule, as run.

  • Loop 0 is the starter lap (radius R about the entry). Loop k+1 moves every moving point of loop k along the streamline of the field (sub-step at most one 0.1 mm cell).
  • The step of each point is the C5 law gap min(s, s'(ρ)) of the NEW loop's own radius at that point (the circle through ± one pass step of arc, as in C15). The steps of all points are one implicit system; a damped iteration solves it to 0.0001 mm.
  • A point stops on a wall or the island where its streamline leaves the region. It also stops when its move cuts no stock (the air stop): this rule is necessary on the pocket.
  • Where two points move apart by more than the tolerance (0.1 mm) the loop gets new points between them. The march ends when every point has stopped.

c·D = 2.175868 mm (c = 0.3626; R 3, s 2, tolerance 0.1 mm, pass step 1.5 mm). Widths are fractions of D; "interior" leaves out R of arc length at the loop seam and at each change between a moving part and a stopped part. "Mean width" is the stock removed divided by the cut length.

Lines: the new cut of each loopthe stopped parts on the walls and the island (every later loop runs along them)the stopped parts in air (the pocket corridor)

3. The five questions

1. One closed loop?

Yes, on both shapes, for every loop (30 on the star, 49 on the pocket). A streamline that reaches the island stops on it, so the loop runs along the near side of the island as it runs along a wall. The loop does not have to split. Behind the island the two fronts come together on the line from the island to the far corner. There the rule must stop a point when its move cuts no stock (the air stop, 267 points). The two fronts then stop on the two sides of a corridor of cleared stock, and every later loop runs up one side and down the other. Without the air stop the points on that line never stop (seen in a trial; the march did not end). The pocket loops cross themselves 4 times, all in loops 48, 49 at x 70.5 to 72.0, y 46.4 to 50.5, where the corridor meets the corner wall.

2. The real gap and load

The lead's prediction holds: the gap normal to the loop is at most the streamline step. Normal gap / step: median 0.979 and smallest 0.792 on the star; median 0.926 and smallest 0.048 on the pocket. More than R from every wall the replay holds the ceiling to within one cell: 0.3622 D star, 0.3741 D pocket (c = 0.3626 D; one cell is 0.0167 D). The interior samples over c (73 star, 38 pocket of 9234 and 12565) all lie within R of a wall. On the star they are on loops 8 to 17, the loops that first reach the walls; the largest is 0.5133 D. Distribution in the interior: median 0.328, 90 % 0.351, 99 % 0.375 D on the star. The normal-gap variant steps farther where the streamline is oblique and reads up to 0.77 D on the pocket.

3. Coverage

The star leaves 56.9 mm²; 55.5 mm² of it is in the five tips, farther than R from every centre position, so no plan cuts it ((e) leaves 57.3 mm²). The pocket leaves 1.73 mm² in one piece at (73.9, 49.4), 1.33 mm from the wall, in the corner where the corridor ends. Where streamlines diverge the loop gets new points at the tolerance, so no wedge stays uncut.

4. Loops and length

Star: 30 loops against 19 levels of (a) and 32 of (e). Cut length 5490 mm: 6.1 times (a) and 1.00 times (e). Pocket: 49 loops, 10313 mm, 8.2 times (a) and 0.98 times (e). The wall and corridor runs are 74% (star) and 82% (pocket) of the length: each loop runs along all the wall that earlier loops reached. The moving part alone is 1.58 times (a) on the star and 1.47 times on the pocket. A straight link across each stopped run instead of the wall run is a lower bound for a shortcut; it still gives 5.0 times (a) on the star.

5. Smoothness

Away from the stops (more than one pass step of arc) the smallest loop radius is 1.98 mm (star) and 2.13 mm (pocket); next to a stop it falls to 0.75 mm. Where a loop leaves a wall it turns by a median 34° and at most 136° (star; pocket 99°) over one pass step: a corner in the loop.

Verdict on the march by cut length. The streamline march does what the lead predicted for the shape: every loop is one closed curve, the load holds away from the walls, and the stock is cut. But it does not remove the overlap. It moves it: the cut length is 1.00 times (e) on the star and 0.98 times on the pocket, because a closed loop must run along all the wall it has reached. Against (a) it is 6.1 times (star) and 8.2 times (pocket). Sections 4 to 6 replace cut length with engaged length, air length and time.

Prediction (not measured): a Rust version would need a field solve, a streamline tracer, the implicit step solve, the air stop on a stock model, and loop resampling; about the size of the C15 (a) level rule plus a stock query per point per loop. The wall runs are a property of a closed loop, not of the implementation, so a Rust version would keep them.

4. Cut parts and link parts (operator addition)

The operator: the overlap of the harmonic plans runs through cleared stock at depth, so it is keep-down travel, not load. So the cut length is the wrong cost. Each plan here is replayed in order with its links. Every sample is engaged when the stock it removes, read as area per mm over one pass step centred on it, is more than one cell width (0.1 mm: the raster's resolution, one cell per cell of path). Every other sample is air.

  • Links. Between two curves the plan takes FreeCAD's rule (R1 §4, ideas only). A link is clear when the tool disc, grown by s·R = 1.00 mm, holds no standing stock. The test starts 2·s·R inside each end. A keep-down route may be up to 3 × the direct length (here, the shortest 8-connected path over the clear nodes, then string pulled to straight segments). A gap shorter than 2·s·R may be cut straight when no step cuts more than 1.5 × c·D per mm. Otherwise the link is a retract.
  • Order. The levels are cut in order. In a level, the next curve is the nearest one. An open arc starts at its nearer end, and a closed loop starts at its nearest point.
  • Feeds. The cut feed is 1500 mm/min (fixture_feeds(Adaptive), compute/fixture_values.rs:34-35; the op has no feed default). The 2D adaptive feeds its own keep-down Link at that same cut feed (adaptive/path.rs:3163-3168, params.feed_rate). A separate link feed exists only in the link-moves dressup: link_feed_rate, default 500 mm/min (compute/config.rs:1077-1083, 1439).
  • Times. The times are for information only: path length over feed, with no acceleration. A retract is counted, not timed.

With the air at the cut feed, (e) and the march take about the same time: 3.67 and 3.67 min on the star, 7.08 and 6.88 min on the pocket. (a) takes 0.63 and 0.88 min, plus 46 and 27 retracts. (e) engages over 2.6 times the length of (a) on the star, so even its engaged part is a thinner cut. At the link-dressup feed the air is 3 times slower than at the cut feed, and (e) takes 7.83 min on the star.

5. One family from (a) to (e) (operator addition)

The family. uλ = (1 − λ)·T/Tmax + λ·uharm, where T is the exact entry distance and uharm is the harmonic field (C15 (e)). Both fields are 0 on the entry disc, and both are scaled to 1 at their far end. λ = 0 is (a) and λ = 1 is (e).

  • Levels. The levels come from the C15 rule: every point of a new level lies within the C5 law gap of its own radius from the cut. Every λ runs until each node lies within one cell of a cut, so every plan clears to the wall. A level line that reaches a wall is cut there into an open arc.
  • The grid. λ steps by 0.05. Below the smallest λ that meets both conditions, the grid gets finer, down to 0.001. This gives 34 values on each shape.
  • λ*. λ* is the λ with the least time at the cut feed that meets (1) no retract and (2) a cut-part interior width of at most c plus one cell. It is computed from the table.
  • Why a linear blend. It is the one-parameter path between the two plans, with no other parameter. A blend that keeps the wall value constant (and so keeps closed loops) is (e) itself. Any λ < 1 gives the wall the value λ + (1 − λ)·T/Tmax, which changes along the wall, so the late levels reach the walls as open arcs.

Result. On both shapes only λ = 1 meets both conditions: λ* = 1.000 (star) and 1.000 (pocket), which is (e). Every λ below 1 has retracts: at least 5 on the star and 14 on the pocket, and 5 and 14 at λ = 0.999. The late levels reach the walls in the lobes and behind the island, and an open arc in a lobe has no keep-down route to the next one. So no λ in the family turns the overlap into only useful links: the plan has either retracts or the air of (e).

How to read the time. A plan below λ* is faster than (e) unless a retract costs more than the break-even time: (time of (e) − time of the plan) / retracts. Over the λ < 1 values that break-even time is 3.7 to 16.6 s per retract on the star and 9.1 to 16.2 s on the pocket. For (a) it is 4.0 s (star) and 13.8 s (pocket). These are at the cut feed with no acceleration, and the retract cost is not measured here.

The streamline march against the family. It has no retract, but its cut parts read 0.4988 D (star) and 0.4396 D (pocket) where a loop leaves a wall, which is above c. So it does not meet condition (2), and it does not beat λ* (march beats the family: star no, pocket no).

6. Keep the loop shape, replace the air runs by links (lead's variant)

Each loop of (e), and of the march, keeps its shape. An air run is a part of the loop that cuts nothing, because an earlier loop already cut it. Each air run is replaced by the shortest keep-down route between its two ends (the rule of section 4) when that route is shorter. This is what the C14 turns do for (a). The loops are cut in their order, and the replay classifies each run against the stock as it is at that moment.

Result.

  • Star. The air runs of (e) lie along the straight walls of the lobes, so no route is shorter. Only 2.7 mm is saved, and (e) stays at 3.66 min.
  • Pocket. The links cross the cleared corners and the area round the island. They save 1580 mm, and (e) takes 6.03 min instead of 7.08 min.
  • The march. Its wall and corridor runs shorten more: 301 mm (star) and 4135 mm (pocket), to 3.47 and 4.12 min. Its cut parts still read 0.5078 D and 0.4396 D, which is over c.
  • Retracts. No retract is added: 0 and 0 for the trimmed (e).
  • Against (a). (a) takes 0.63 and 0.88 min, with 46 and 27 retracts. The trimmed (e) is faster only if a retract costs more than 4.0 s (star) or 11.4 s (pocket).

The rest of the extra time of (e) is engaged path, not air: (e) engages 2.6 and 2.9 times the length of (a), because its thin loops cut little stock per mm. No change to the links can remove that.

Overall verdict. The march is not a candidate for Rust. With the air counted as keep-down travel it takes the time of (e) (1.00 and 0.97 times (e) at the cut feed), but its cut parts read over c where a loop leaves a wall. In the family from (a) to (e), only (e) has no retract and holds c in its cut parts, so λ* is (e) on both shapes. Links in place of the air runs of (e) save little on the star and 1580 mm on the pocket; most of the extra time of (e) is engaged path. The choice between (e) and (a) with its retracts depends on what a retract costs, which this prototype does not measure: (a) is faster unless a retract costs more than 4.0 s (star) or 13.8 s (pocket) against (e), or 4.0 s and 11.4 s against the trimmed (e).
